statement: Are there positive integers a and b, both greater than 4, with one over a plus one over b equal to one half?

choices.misconception: I guessed a pair without checking that one fifth plus one fifth is less than one half.
I picked equal values whose sum is one third rather than one half.

choices.text: Yes, but only with a and b different
choices.misconception: I assumed unequal values could rescue a sum that is already too small.

choices.text: No, because the sum would be less than one half
No, because one half cannot be written as such a sum at all
choices.misconception: I overstated the obstacle, since 1/3 + 1/6 and 1/4 + 1/4 both work.

hints: If both numbers exceed 4, then each fraction is at most one fifth, so bound the sum and compare it with one half. A bound that already fails rules out every pair at once.
Each of a and b being at least 5 makes each fraction at most one fifth, so the sum is at most two fifths.

solutions.reliable: If a and b are both at least 5 then each reciprocal is at most 1/5, so the sum is at most 2/5, which is below 1/2. No such pair exists. The transferable idea: bound the expression before searching, because a bound that already fails disposes of infinitely many cases in one line.
solutions.elegant: Two fifths is less than a half, so there is nothing left to check.

whyOnTest: Bounding replaces an endless search, and the distractors are all pairs a student would try before thinking to bound.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
